tagline.text: A waterfall park in the heart of Antipolo with a legend of a thrown bell

location.label: Location
location.text: Taktak Road, Barangay Dela Paz, Antipolo, Rizal

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: November–May dry season (more water in the rainy season, but paths are slippery)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱100–500 (transport, parking and snacks, per person)

children.text: Hinulugang Taktak is a protected park in central Antipolo built around a waterfall about 21.5 meters high and 25.8 meters wide. Its name comes from a legend of a bell thrown into the falls, and at about 1.7 kilometers from the cathedral it pairs easily into a day trip.

Hinulugang Taktak is a waterfall and park in the middle of Antipolo, Rizal. The park covers about 3.2 hectares, and the falls are listed as about 21.5 meters high and 25.8 meters wide. It is now a protected area managed jointly by the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) and the Rizal provincial government, and at about 21 kilometers from Manila it is easy to visit in a day. It lies about 1.7 kilometers from Antipolo Cathedral along Taktak Road, and together with the cathedral it is regarded as one of Antipolo's two best-known sights.

The name comes with a legend. In the 15th or 16th century, villagers are said to have thrown a large bell (taktak) into the falls because it was too loud, and the name is read as roughly "the place where the bell fell." The falls also appear in the 1929 song "Antipolo" by German San Jose, which is cited as evidence that people were already going there for recreation. Five lots were reserved as a recreation area on July 15, 1952, it became a national park in 1990, and in 2000 it became a protected landscape run by the DENR and the Rizal provincial government.

The falls were once known for pollution. The water began to decline in the 1960s, and by about 1998 around 75 percent of the area had been restored, but the river is still described as unsafe for swimming. That is why the park has a separate swimming pool. In 2015 an oil spill closed it for eleven days before it reopened, and on February 13, 2020 it reopened after about a year of rehabilitation with new facilities such as a spider web platform, hanging bridges and a wall-climbing facility. Recorded visitors reached about 843,000 in 2018, so it is popular locally. Rehabilitation began in 1991 and cost more than 45 million pesos by 1998, and in 2009 a three-year budget of 100 million pesos was set. Private institutions also helped with photo exhibits, bamboo planting and re-greening. Visitors rose from about 45,000 in 1995 to about 83,000 in 2004, and in 2004 it was recorded as the second most popular national park in the country. In 2008 it earned about 11.1 million pesos, the third-largest income among Philippine protected areas.

This guide is for travelers who want to spend a day combining the park with Antipolo Cathedral and the Pinto Art Museum. If you expect a big nature attraction you may be disappointed, but its appeal is that you can hear a waterfall and take a walk in the middle of a city. Admission fees, hours and which facilities are open change often, so check the latest announcements. Do not assume the water is clean, and you will be happier if you think of it as a place to look at rather than get into. The bedrock is said to be Miocene layers beneath Quaternary soil, and areas near the slopes are vulnerable to erosion and landslides. Knowing this background turns it from simple waterfall viewing into a trip that also reads the history of a city and nature pressing against each other.
The falls, about
high and

wide, are the center of the park. From the viewing areas you can see them from the front and the side, and in the rainy season the flow grows and the sound is loud. The river water is described as unsuitable for swimming, so enjoy it with your eyes only. The park is small, about 3.2 hectares, so a slow walk around the falls takes about an hour. By IUCN classification it is described as a protected landscape (Category V).

The legend that villagers threw a large bell into the falls is the origin of the name. It is not a verified story, but it is a fun way to understand local culture. Read together with the record that the falls appear in the song "Antipolo" (1929), it shows that these falls have been a playground for Antipolo residents for nearly a century.
Swimming in the river is dangerous, so the park provides a separate swimming pool. A children's water area and a meditation area are also described. Check fees and hours locally.

The park is small, but its trees are thick, so it makes a short walk even in the middle of the city. At least eleven tree species are known, including mahogany, narra, ylang-ylang and mango. Animals such as the Asian water monitor and the flying lizard are said to live here, so walk quietly on the forest paths.

blocks.title: Hanging bridges and the spider web platform

children.text: When the park reopened in 2020, hanging bridges, a spider web platform and a wall-climbing facility were added. However, there are reports that some of them are under maintenance or closed, so check before you go. If you are hoping for photos looking down on the falls from above, check local announcements first.
The cathedral is about
1.7 km

away, so you can make the short trip by tricycle. Seeing the cathedral in the morning and walking in the waterfall park after lunch makes a satisfying half day. Together they let you see Antipolo's two symbols at once. The roads are hilly, so on hot days take a tricycle or Grab rather than walking.

The park sits at the headwaters of the Sapang Baho River (also called the Antipolo River or the Taktak River), and the water flows through the Manggahan Floodway to Laguna de Bay. In an urbanized setting you can see surviving forest and water, so many families with children come. No endangered species have been specially reported, but it is meaningful that such woodland remains in a city.
Leave Manila and reach central Antipolo by LRT-2 Antipolo Station, taxi or Grab.
Check the fee and parking at the park entrance, go in, and see the falls viewing area first.
Walk slowly through the forest paths, bridges and the pool area. Check which facilities are open.
Head into town for lunch.
Take a tricycle about
1.7 km
to look around Antipolo Cathedral.
Whether facilities in the park are open changes often, so ask staff at the entrance which areas are available today to save travel time. On weekends the entry line can get long.
Spend the morning at Hinulugang Taktak park.
Look around Antipolo Cathedral and the plaza stalls.
Have lunch, then go to the Pinto Art Museum for the afternoon.
Ride LRT-2 to Antipolo Station, then take a jeepney or tricycle up toward town. From the station to the park it can take
20–40 minutes
depending on traffic.
LRT-2 extensions and stations can change, so check the latest route map before you leave.
Buses and jeepneys to Antipolo run from Cubao and Quiapo. The terminus is said to be near Robinsons in town, and from there you take a tricycle.
The park is on Taktak Road in Barangay Dela Paz, which branches off Sumulong Highway.
Enter central Antipolo by Marcos Highway or Ortigas Avenue Extension and head to Taktak Road.
On weekends the park entrance and roads are crowded, so arriving early at opening time makes parking easier.
Tricycles and Grab are convenient between the cathedral, the park and the Pinto Art Museum. Negotiate the fare or check the app screen.

The falls can be seen year-round, but in rainy periods the flow increases and the paths are slippery. The dry season from December to April is easier for travel and walking, though the flow may be lower.
May overlaps with the pilgrimage season at Antipolo Cathedral, and the whole city is crowded. On weekday mornings it is quiet, and on weekends many families visit.

For photos, the morning right after opening is best, and the day after rain the flow thickens and the impression changes a lot. On the other hand, after days of heavy rain the river is muddy and paths can be dangerous, so check the weather forecast before planning.

Antipolo is a day trip from Manila, so most travelers stay in Manila or Quezon City. There are hotels and resorts near the park, but options and rates vary by season, so check recent reviews on booking sites.

Food is found at stalls around the park and at restaurants in town. In front of the cathedral you can buy roasted cashews and kalamay, and restaurants along Sumulong Highway are described as offering city views while you dine. For street food, choose stalls where you can see the hygiene for yourself.

If you plan to stay in the park a long time, bring water and snacks. The park has picnic tables and cottages, and past fee schedules are described as having hourly rental rates, so families should check locally. There may be few trash cans, so bring a bag to carry out your waste.
Going at opening time is quiet and good for photos.

Carry out your trash and do not leave it at the falls or in the forest.

In the rainy season paths are slippery and torrents can form, so do not go past railings.
